doc.title: Dave Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Theory and improvising in trad jazz versus modal styles
summary: Trad improvisation is melody-based with set changes, which is harder for young players used to modal playing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay I’m curious as to how much music theory you feel is appropriate or necessary for kids to know to improvise in traditional jazz.

Well you certainly have to know the basics, you have to know your scales and chords. But I would say it relies — I don’t know, I’m going to get in trouble no matter what I say — but I would say it relies less on, it’s not so much modal playing. You know there’s a lot of modal scales that people here at this conference are teaching to young people that are needed for the later styles of jazz. For these styles it’s really more melody-based I think, and the changes, the chord changes tend to be simpler. But I find that that’s actually a bigger challenge in a lot of cases for young players, because it is a smaller box to work within and when you have a sort of a droning flat eleven chord going on for a while you get away with a lot of different things, in fact you’re expected really to step outside of that and play dissonant things and so forth. It’s in some ways easier to get away with playing a solo in that kind of a setting than in a setting where you’ve got a set of changes, you know a 32-bar structure, a set of changes and a bridge or a multi-strain piece that changes key and so forth and you’ve got to stay within that and a wrong note sounds like a wrong note.

It’s just a whole different bag. So in my band I’ve had a lot of players come in highly recommended that, boy they’re really hot players, but some of them, you know you ask them to play a simple 32-bar tune, like “I Got Rhythm” or something, and they’re kind of all over the place.
Do they have trouble remembering where they are in the song while they’re trying to improvise?

Sometimes. I think it’s more just following the chord structure and staying within that and connecting the chords in a way that makes sense, playing a melodic line that makes sense. And for the earlier styles playing a line that makes sense stylistically and is not
using phrasing that’s really outside of that genre. The young people just for the most part have not been exposed to the earlier styles.
